analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover COVID-19 testing with no copays, deductibles, or prior approval.
analysis.headline: The bill got no hearing or vote in any of the three committees it was sent to and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required private health insurance plans to pay for COVID-19 testing in full during the declared public health emergency — no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance, and no prior-approval hoops that could delay a test. It also covered the doctor's office, urgent care, or emergency room visit connected to getting tested. The bill went to three House committees the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with private health insurance who needed a COVID-19 test during the emergency: they would pay nothing out of pocket for the test, its administration, or the related visit, and insurers could not require prior authorization before covering it.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and individual and group insurance to cover approved COVID-19 tests and their administration with no cost sharing — no deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance — for the duration of the emergency declared January 31, 2020.

Also bans prior authorization and other utilization-management requirements, so an insurer could not slow down or gatekeep a test, and covers the related office, urgent care, and emergency room visits.
Enforced by the Secretaries of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury through the same rules that govern other insurance coverage requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would bear the full cost of testing and related visits during the emergency, a cost likely reflected in premiums; the mandate reached only insured people, not the uninsured.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to people with private insurance, leaving the uninsured — often the people least able to pay — outside its protection.
Insurers and employers funding group plans would absorb testing and visit costs, which tends to flow into premiums over time.
The requirement was temporary, tied to the emergency period, and it applied only to testing — not to treatment if the test came back positive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Free, gatekeeper-free testing during a pandemic is a clear public benefit, and the cost to insurers was modest relative to the public-health value of finding cases early. Its real limits were coverage: it excluded the uninsured and did not touch treatment costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Frederica Wilson of Florida introduced the bill on March 11, 2020, joined by 17 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees, and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No committee took it up; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote after the referral, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who fund group plans avoided a no-cost-sharing testing mandate from this bill, which never advanced beyond committee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have required insurers to pay the full cost of COVID-19 tests and related visits without imposing copays or prior approval, shifting those costs from patients to insurers and the plans they administer. The bill never advanced, so insurers avoided this mandate from it.

industries.industry: COVID-19 test makers and diagnostic labs
industries.note: Insurers would have been required to cover approved tests and their administration, guaranteeing payment for test manufacturers and labs. More people getting tested with no out-of-pocket cost means more paid claims.
